quartiers:The palace.name: The palace
quartiers:The palace.teaser: Four Roman gates, one colonnaded court, and washing lines strung between 1,700-year-old walls
quartiers:The palace.story: Diocletian built this as his retirement house; when Salona fell in the 7th century its people moved inside the walls and never left. Today you enter by one of four gates: Golden to the north, Silver to the east by the Pazar, Bronze from the sea, Iron to the west. All four lanes lead to the Peristyle, where red granite columns frame the cathedral steps. One alley off, the palace turns domestic: a scooter against a Roman pilaster, laundry over a medieval window. How many still live here is argued: 3,000 is the usual figure, Fodor's says just over 1,000 and falling as flats become rentals.
quartiers:The palace.why: Walk it twice: once at first light, empty, and once after the cruise passengers have gone back aboard.
facts: The Roman gates, the Peristyle, and the lanes where people still hang their washing

quartiers:Veli Varoš.name: Veli Varoš
quartiers:Veli Varoš.teaser: Steep stone lanes west of the palace, where Split's fishermen lived and the konobas still cook
quartiers:Veli Varoš.story: West of the Riva the streets tilt up toward Marjan. Veli Varoš grew outside the walls around the little church of St Nicholas, Sveti Mikula, which the tourist board calls perhaps the best preserved medieval church in Split; the hamlet then was Stagnja. Until recently this was the fishermen's quarter: low stone houses, outside stairs, lanes too narrow and steep for a car. The parish of the Holy Cross, Sveti Križ, has kept its feast on 14 September for some six centuries. It is also a byword for the fetivi, the old Split families with their famously fast talk, as against boduli from the islands and vlaji from the hinterland.

quartiers:The Riva and Matejuška.name: The Riva and Matejuška
quartiers:The Riva and Matejuška.teaser: Palms, white paving and the palace's sea wall, ending at a harbour full of small wooden fishing boats
quartiers:The Riva and Matejuška.story: The Riva runs along the palace's south wall, where the sea once lapped the Bronze Gate. Its central stretch was rebuilt in 2006-2007; the digging turned up a Roman sea wall and landing platform in front of the palace. Behind the cafés, the Prokurative (Trg Republike) opens to the water through neo-Renaissance arcades on three sides, begun in 1859 with a theatre at its centre that burned in 1882. At the western end the paving gives way to Matejuška, the fishermen's harbour, where small wooden boats are pulled up on the stone and men mend nets. The ferries for Brač and Hvar pull out across the bay.

quartiers:Bačvice and Firule.name: Bačvice and Firule
quartiers:Bačvice and Firule.teaser: Sand underfoot ten minutes from the palace, then a quieter pine-backed bay where locals swim
quartiers:Bačvice and Firule.story: Walk east past the ferry and cruise terminal and the city opens onto its own beaches. In late autumn several beach bars close or cut their hours from November: check the season.

curiosities:The sphinx on the peristyle.name: The sphinx on the Peristyle
curiosities:The sphinx on the peristyle.teaser: A black granite sphinx about 3,500 years old, brought from Egypt by the emperor and still on guard
curiosities:The sphinx on the peristyle.story: Most visitors photograph the columns and walk past it. Low against the cathedral side of the Peristyle lies a black granite sphinx, about two and a half metres long, carved in Egypt in the 15th century BC and usually linked to Thutmose III. Diocletian had put down a revolt in Egypt around 297 and shipped home a dozen or more sphinxes to line his new palace. Only a few survive: this one, a headless one in front of the Temple of Jupiter, and a third in the City Museum. Who smashed the rest is not recorded.
curiosities:The sphinx on the peristyle.why: It is older than Rome itself: put a hand on the oldest object in the city.
facts: Come after 23:30 on a November night, when the terraces have packed up: sit on the steps under the Vestibule, and the granite is cold and the court is silent

curiosities:Grgur Ninski's toe.name: Grgur Ninski's toe
curiosities:Grgur Ninski's toe.teaser: Rub the bishop's big toe, not his thumb: the bronze has been polished gold by millions of hands
curiosities:Grgur Ninski's toe.story: Outside the Golden Gate a bronze bishop some eight metres tall raises his finger at the sky. Ivan Meštrović made Grgur Ninski in 1929 for the medieval bishop of Nin who fought for the Slavonic liturgy against Latin, and first set him in the middle of the Peristyle. During the Second World War he was taken down, and only in the 1950s was he raised again outside the palace's north gate. The custom is to rub his big toe for luck, and the toe now shines bright gold against the dark green bronze. Several guidebooks still say thumb: it is the toe.
curiosities:Grgur Ninski's toe.why: Make a wish on the toe on your way in through the Golden Gate.
facts: Rub the big toe of the left foot, then walk through the Golden Gate into the palace

curiosities:No flies in the fish hall.name: No flies in the fish hall
curiosities:No flies in the fish hall.teaser: A hall full of fresh fish in summer, and, so Split insists, not a single fly
curiosities:No flies in the fish hall.story: Stand by the Ribarnica, Peškarija in dialect, on a July morning and notice what is missing: the flies. The story every Splićanin will tell you is that the sulphur springs next door keep them off. The springs are real. The Art Nouveau spa building of 1903 at the end of Marmontova stands over waters used as a cure since the 18th century, and on some days you can smell them. Local lore even claims the springs drew Diocletian here. Whether sulphur actually keeps insects out of a fish market is another matter: we found the claim repeated, never tested.
curiosities:No flies in the fish hall.why: Go early, look and sniff for yourself: the fish is the reason, the riddle is a bonus.

curiosities:The stone of the White House.name: The stone of the White House
curiosities:The stone of the White House.teaser: Brač stone built Diocletian's palace. Whether it ever reached Washington is another story
curiosities:The stone of the White House.story: Every guide on this coast tells you the White House is built of Brač stone. It was not. Its walls were raised in 1792-1799 from Aquia Creek sandstone, quarried in Virginia and painted white. The Brač version shrinks on inspection to a claim that island stone went into a 1902 renovation, or into a fireplace, backed by a shipping receipt nobody cites; the islanders say the quarry records were destroyed in the war. The palace you are standing in is different: Split's City Museum says it was built almost entirely of Brač limestone, cut near Škrip and shipped from Splitska.
curiosities:The stone of the White House.why: Trust the palace wall under your hand, not the Washington story.
facts: Lay a palm on the palace's south wall on the Riva: that pale stone came across the channel from Brač 1,700 years ago

curiosities:Picigin.name: Picigin
curiosities:Picigin.teaser: Knee-deep water, a small ball, and one rule: it must never touch the sea
curiosities:Picigin.story: At Bačvice grown men dive full length into knee-deep water to save a ball. That is picigin: players stand in a loose ring and slap a small ball to one another with the flat of the hand, and the only rule that matters is that it must not land in the sea. There is no score and no winner, only the save. It was first played here in 1908, the story goes, by students home from university who found water polo hopeless in such shallow water. In 2013 Croatia's Ministry of Culture listed it as intangible heritage, and Bačvice hosts a picigin world championship.
curiosities:Picigin.why: Watch one late-afternoon game: the dives into ankle-deep water are the point.
facts: Stand at the water's edge at Bačvice on a warm afternoon; in late October games are rarer, but locals still play on mild days

culture:The substructures.name: The substructures
culture:The substructures.teaser: The emperor's floor plan, preserved in the dark: vaulted halls where Daenerys kept her dragons
culture:The substructures.story: Diocletian's apartments stood above the sea on a vaulted cellar storey that copied the rooms above, hall for hall. The apartments are gone; the cellars are almost entirely preserved and show the emperor's plan in cool, damp stone: long vaulted halls, dripping water, the smell of wet limestone. The central passage from the Bronze Gate is free, lined with stalls; the side halls are ticketed. Game of Thrones used them in season 4 as the vaults where Daenerys chains her dragons. The palace, 215 by 180 metres, built 295-305, is UNESCO-listed since 1979.

culture:The cathedral and its bell tower.name: The cathedral and its bell tower
culture:The cathedral and its bell tower.teaser: The emperor built himself a tomb; the city turned it into a cathedral for a bishop he had executed
culture:The cathedral and its bell tower.story: Diocletian, persecutor of Christians, built this octagonal mausoleum for himself. Domnius, bishop of Salona, was executed in 304 under him, as tradition records it. In the 7th century the refugees from Salona consecrated the emperor's tomb to Domnius, now Split's patron, Sveti Duje. Andrija Buvina carved the wooden doors in 1214. The Romanesque bell tower, about 57 metres, was heavily restored in 1890-1908; its stairs reopened in 2020 after two years of repair. From the top the Roman grid of the palace is still plain, with Mosor (1,339 m) behind.

culture:The Archaeological Museum.name: The Archaeological Museum
culture:The Archaeological Museum.teaser: Croatia's oldest museum, founded 1820: Salona's sarcophagi arranged around a quiet garden courtyard
culture:The Archaeological Museum.story: Most of what Salona left behind came here. Founded in 1820 and usually called the oldest museum in Croatia, it keeps its best pieces outdoors in a courtyard lapidarium under arcades: Roman tombstones, inscriptions and two marble sarcophagi from the Manastirine cemetery at Salona, both from the early 4th century. One shows the Greek myth of Hippolytus and Phaedra; the other, the Good Shepherd, puts Christ as a shepherd at its centre, made for Salona's newly Christian elite. Inside are finds from Greek Issa on Vis and the Illyrian hinterland. It is a short walk north of the palace and rarely crowded.

provisioning:Paški sir and Pag salt.name: Paški sir and Pag salt
provisioning:Paški sir and Pag salt.teaser: Pag's sheep cheese and Pag's sea salt, both shaped by the bura: buy them in Split, three hours south
provisioning:Paški sir and Pag salt.story: Pag is a long bare island of stone and sheep about three hours north of Split by road. When the bura blows from the north-east it throws salt spray across the scrub the sheep graze on, and the old guide hears that salt in the milk. Paški sir, hard-pressed and aged for months, became an EU protected designation of origin in November 2019. The island's salt pans are older still: a will of 999 is cited as the first written record of salt production, and under Venice most of the harvest went to the Republic. Solana Pag is now Croatia's largest sea-salt producer.

walks:Salona and Klis.teaser: The Roman capital of Dalmatia in the Solin fields, then up to the fortress that guarded the pass
walks:Salona and Klis.story: Before Split there was Salona, capital of Roman Dalmatia, a few kilometres north in what is now Solin. calas:Bačvice.name: Bačvice
calas:Bačvice.teaser: Split's sandy town beach, shallow far out: at six in the morning it belongs to the fishermen
calas:Bačvice.story: Bačvice is a rarity on a coast of pebbles: a shallow bay of sand, ten minutes' walk east of the palace, where you can wade thirty metres out and still stand waist-deep. In summer it is the stage for picigin, which has its own card. Come at six instead. Walk past the changing cabins to the pebble point at the east end, where a fisherman or two may be mending nets. The sun comes up over Mosor, and Hvar turns pale pink across the channel. In late October the sea has cooled to about 18-20°C.
calas:Bačvice.why: The 06:00 hour, when the beach is empty and the light comes off the mountain.
facts: About 10 minutes on foot east from the Riva, past the ferry port

calas:Kašjuni.name: Kašjuni
calas:Kašjuni.teaser: A pebble beach under the cliffs on Marjan's south shore, with no road to the water's edge
calas:Kašjuni.story: Kašjuni lies on Marjan's south shore, west of the Meštrović Gallery, where the pine slopes come down to a long curve of pale pebbles and very clear water. No car reaches the shore, so it stays quieter than the town beaches. In summer there are sunbeds from the beach bar, showers and changing cabins. By late October the bar and the loungers are packed away for the season and the sea is near 20°C and falling. A swim then is short, cold and very clear.
calas:Kašjuni.why: Clearer water than any beach in town, ten minutes by bus from the Riva.

calas:Bene.name: Bene
calas:Bene.teaser: A shaded swim on Marjan's north shore, where the pines reach almost to the rocks
calas:Bene.story: Bene is the beach at the end of the Marjan walk, on the hill's north shore, where the pines grow almost to the waterline and there is shade for most of the day. Behind the rocks are a café-restaurant, showers, tennis courts and a playground, so local families come in summer. It is the place to finish the hill loop with a swim, then take the bus back. In late October the facilities run short hours or close, the water is around 20°C, and you may have the shore to yourself.

around:Brač.name: Brač
around:Brač.teaser: Fifty minutes by car ferry to Supetar, then across the island to Bol and the white spit of Zlatni Rat
around:Brač.story: The car ferry pulls out of Split harbour and fifty minutes later ties up in Supetar, a low town of pale stone on Brač's north shore. From there the road crosses the island's high karst, dry-stone walls and olive terraces, then drops down to Bol on the south coast. Just west of Bol runs Zlatni Rat, a spit of white pebbles reaching into the channel, its tip shifting with wind and current. The island is quarried limestone through and through: the stone's travels and the stonemasons' school at Pučišća have their own cards, as does the Stina cellar on Bol's waterfront.
around:Brač.why: Zlatni Rat seen from the water or the path above, with Hvar across the channel.

around:Hvar and Vis.name: Hvar and Vis
around:Hvar and Vis.teaser: Greek field walls on Hvar, and Vis, the island closed to outsiders until 1989
around:Hvar and Vis.story: Hvar is the long island south of Brač. Its town has the harbour and the crowds, but the older wonder is inland: the Stari Grad plain, fields laid out by Greek colonists in the 4th century BC and farmed ever since, their stone boundaries still in place, a UNESCO site since 2008. Vis lies further out, the most distant inhabited island off the coast. Yugoslavia kept it as a naval base and closed it to foreigners until 1989; the army only left around 1992. The isolation kept Vis town and Komiža quiet. Eat a viška pogača there and drink a Vugava, both told elsewhere in this guide.
around:Hvar and Vis.why: Vis: an island that missed the tourist decades because the army held it.
facts: Hvar: Jadrolinija car ferry to Stari Grad; catamarans to Hvar town run about twice a day in winter (Oct 2026 listings). Vis: Jadrolinija line 602 sails year-round on a reduced winter timetable from late September. Check every sailing in November
A full day for either; Vis is better with a night

around:Trogir.name: Trogir
around:Trogir.teaser: A walled medieval town on its own islet, and Master Radovan's carved portal of 1240
around:Trogir.story: Trogir sits on a small island between the mainland and Čiovo, joined to both by bridges. Inside the walls, the lanes are narrower, darker and quieter than Split's. At the centre the Cathedral of St Lawrence keeps its west door, signed by Master Radovan in 1240: Adam and Eve stand on lions, and around the arch run the months of the year, peasants slaughtering pigs and pressing grapes. Venice held the town from 1420 to 1797, and you see it in the Cipiko palace windows and the Kamerlengo fortress on the waterfront. UNESCO listed the whole town in 1997.
around:Trogir.why: Radovan's portal: stand close and read the farming year carved into the stone.

around:Omiš and the Cetina.name: Omiš and the Cetina
around:Omiš and the Cetina.teaser: A town wedged in the Cetina gorge, where pirate dukes once charged ships for safe passage
around:Omiš and the Cetina.story: Omiš sits where the Cetina breaks out of a limestone gorge into the sea, the cliffs rising straight behind the rooftops. In the 12th and 13th centuries the Kačić family ruled here and their galleys made the channels to the south dangerous for any ship that had not paid. Their lookout was Mirabella, a 13th-century tower above the old town that watched the Brač channel; the higher fortress of Starigrad, or Fortica, is about an hour's climb. Upriver the canyon narrows into green water and sheer walls, rafted in summer. The klapa festival is the calendar's.
around:Omiš and the Cetina.why: Climb Mirabella: the gorge mouth and the channel the pirates watched, both from one wall.
facts: About 25 minutes by car south-east along the coast road (old guide)
Half a day; a full day with the canyon

avoid:The cruise-day midday.name: The cruise-day midday
avoid:The cruise-day midday.teaser: When several ships are in, the palace lanes jam from mid-morning to mid-afternoon: move your day around it
avoid:The cruise-day midday.story: Split is a cruise port and the ships dock a few minutes' walk from the palace. On a day with several calls, the tenders and shuttles empty onto the Riva in waves, guided groups follow raised flags through the Peristyle and the cardo, and the narrow lanes stop moving. The same stones that were empty at seven are shoulder to shoulder by eleven, and stay that way until the passengers are recalled in the afternoon. The pressure eases from late October as the season winds down, but a fine day with two or three big ships can still fill the old town.
avoid:The cruise-day midday.why: The palace is a different place before nine and after six: plan the walking for then and the lunch for elsewhere.

avoid:The laminated menu in the palace.name: The laminated menu in the palace
avoid:The laminated menu in the palace.teaser: Photo menus in five languages and a peka on the table in fifteen minutes: neither was made for you
avoid:The laminated menu in the palace.story: Peka is cooked slowly under an iron bell buried in embers, lamb or octopus with potatoes, and a kitchen that does it properly needs to know you are coming. So when a terrace inside the palace walls offers peka at around 28 euros, ready in a quarter of an hour, from a laminated board of faded photographs translated into five languages, the arithmetic does not work. Whatever arrives was cooked earlier for someone else, or not under a bell at all. The dish itself is The Dish's to explain; the warning here is about the menu that sells it.
avoid:The laminated menu in the palace.why: A peka is ordered the day before, not pointed at on a photograph.
facts: On the palace terraces: laminated photo menus in five languages, a waiter at the door, and peka listed as if it could be ordered on the spot (about EUR 28, seen May 2026)

avoid:The pitcher of house wine.name: The pitcher of house wine
avoid:The pitcher of house wine.teaser: An unlabelled jug on a Peristyle terrace, priced like Plavac Mali: ask what is in it, or ask for a bottle
avoid:The pitcher of house wine.story: Some terraces around the Peristyle pour their house wine from an anonymous jug, with no producer, grape or region on the menu, and charge for it as if it were a named Dalmatian red. Nobody at the table can tell you what it is or where it came from, and that is the problem: you are paying a coastal price for wine you cannot trace. Dalmatia makes plenty of honest bottles, and a labelled Plavac Mali or Pošip by the glass is rarely much dearer. If the waiter cannot name the grape or the cellar, take that as the answer.
avoid:The pitcher of house wine.why: A name on the label is the cheapest quality check in Split.
facts: On the palace terraces: house wine by the jug or carafe, no producer or grape named, priced close to a labelled Plavac Mali

avoid:Pašticada in August.name: Pašticada in August
avoid:Pašticada in August.teaser: A winter Sunday braise on a July menu by the Riva: in the heat, ask who made it and when
avoid:Pašticada in August.story: Pašticada is a slow dish: beef marinated for a day, then braised for hours in wine and prunes until the sauce turns dark and glossy. It belongs to cold months and long family Sundays. In July and August, when the palace and Riva menus all list it at around 25 euros, few kitchens are starting one from raw meat in a hot room, and what comes to the table has usually been reheated. The dish deserves better. The Dish card tells its story; this card only says when and where not to order it.
avoid:Pašticada in August.why: Order it where a named kitchen makes it, or come back for it in November.
facts: On the Riva and palace menus in July and August: pašticada listed at about EUR 25 (seen May 2026) with no sign of when it was cooked

follow:Jadrolinija.teaser: The state ferry line to Brač, Hvar, Vis and Šolta: from autumn the timetable thins, so check it daily
follow:Jadrolinija.story: Jadrolinija runs the car ferries and catamarans from Split harbour to the islands. Its site carries the timetables, fares and service notices, and the notices matter most. listening:Klapa.name: Klapa
listening:Klapa.teaser: A small group of voices in a tight half-circle under the open dome, no instruments, the stone doing the rest
listening:Klapa.story: Klapa is Dalmatia's unaccompanied multipart song: a small group led by a first tenor, standing close in a semicircle, singing of the sea, love and home, learned by ear. UNESCO inscribed it on its Representative List of intangible heritage in 2012. In Split the place to hear it is the Vestibule, the round, roofless hall above the Peristyle, where the dome's open eye and bare stone carry the voices up and hold them. In June and September 2026 the Tourist Board listed Monday promenade concerts by KUDŽ Filip Dević, Piva klapa isp'o volta, moving between the Vestibule, Pjaca and the Golden Gate. The Omiš klapa festival is on the calendar.
listening:Klapa.why: Stand inside the Vestibule while a klapa sings: the room is the instrument.
facts: Summer evenings; in 2026 the promenade concerts ran Mondays at 20:00 in June and September (Visit Split). In late October check the events calendar: the series is seasonal
The Vestibule above the Peristyle, plus Pjaca and the Golden Gate on promenade nights

listening:Oliver Dragojević.name: Oliver Dragojević
listening:Oliver Dragojević.teaser: The island boy whose warm, cracked voice still plays in every konoba from Split to Korčula
listening:Oliver Dragojević.story: Oliver Dragojević was born on 7 December 1947 and grew up in Vela Luka on Korčula, the fishing town his family came from, before they moved to Split when his father took a job at the port. For four decades his voice, low and slightly rough, carried the Dalmatian pop song: the sea, the gulls, the one who left. He died in Split on 29 July 2018, after a year with lung cancer. A week later Trogir painted a 25-metre mural of him with seagulls and a line from Moj galebe. In March 2026 Vela Luka set an installation shaped like his early spectacles by the sea.
listening:Oliver Dragojević.why: Play him on deck at dusk and the whole crew will know the chorus by the second night.
facts: 7 December 1947, in Split according to most sources; others say in Vela Luka, where he grew up

listening:Gibonni.name: Gibonni
listening:Gibonni.teaser: A Split metal kid who became the coast's songwriter, and wrote Oliver's best-loved ballad
listening:Gibonni.story: Zlatan Stipišić, Gibonni, was born in Split on 13 August 1968, the son of Ljubo Stipišić, a composer and poet. He started in the 1980s singing heavy metal with the Split band Osmi Putnik, moved to Divlje Jagode, where a bandmate gave him the nickname, then went solo in the early 1990s. His songs mix Dalmatian melody with rock and a dry, plain-spoken lyric. He wrote Cesarica for Oliver Dragojević, and it became one of the best-known Croatian songs of its decade. In 2003 he became a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador.

craft:Do this one.name: Kameni otok, Postira (Brač)
craft:Do this one.teaser: Two hours with a point, a claw chisel and a block of the white Brač limestone the palace is made of
craft:Do this one.story: Brač has been cutting its white limestone since the Romans quarried it for Diocletian, and the craft never stopped: the stonemasons' school at Pučišća has taught hand carving since 1909 and still sends students to win prizes at the Verona stone fair. On the north coast at Postira, a small outfit called Kameni otok, stone island, sits a few visitors at a bench with the real tools: point, claw chisel, hammer. A certified master stonemason guides your hand while the dust settles white on your sleeves, and you leave with the piece you cut. Missing: the master is not named in any listing we found.
craft:Do this one.why: The only hands-on craft near Split you can book like a table, and it uses the stone you have been walking on all week.

craft:Other two.name: The Benedictine nuns of Hvar

craft:Other two.story: Behind a plain wall in Hvar town, in the house that once belonged to the Renaissance poet Hanibal Lucić, Benedictine nuns have lived since 1664. They make lace from fibres drawn out of the long grey-green leaves of the agave that grows on the island: the pale threads are pulled free and worked into stiff ivory medallions, weeks each. craft:What is sold as Dalmatian craft.name: What is sold as Dalmatian craft
craft:What is sold as Dalmatian craft.teaser: Cheap 'Hvar lace' and shiny 'filigree' in the palace alleys rarely came off a Dalmatian bench
craft:What is sold as Dalmatian craft.story: Between the Peristyle and the Riva the same crafts repeat on every stall: lace, silver filigree, white stone. Each is slow by nature. Real Hvar agave lace is made by one convent of nuns, a medallion over weeks, so a pile of cheap 'Hvar lace' on a stall cannot be theirs. A pair of hand-made filigree earrings costs a Split craftsman eight or nine hours, which is why most jewellery sold as filigree is now cast in a mould. If a seller cannot name the maker and the place, assume nobody here made it.
craft:What is sold as Dalmatian craft.why: Ask who made it and where; the real makers in this section answer with a name.
facts: Turn the piece over: hand filigree shows tiny solder joints and slightly uneven loops, cast work is smooth and identical; agave lace is stiff and ivory, not soft white cotton. Ask the seller for the maker's name

linger:D16 Coffee.teaser: Split's own specialty roaster, in a dim palace alley with a few tables on the stone outside
linger:D16 Coffee.story: D16 roasts its own beans and pours them in a small, low room on Dominisova, a lane inside the palace's western half, with a handful of tables in the alley outside. This is the cup locals point to when you ask for coffee rather than a terrace: a V60 of a rotating Ethiopian single origin, a proper espresso, a cold brew in the heat. The room is dark and the music can run loud, so for real work use the second, larger D16 at Trogirska 8, just outside the walls. Old notes that placed it at Dosud 9 were wrong.
linger:D16 Coffee.why: The best filter coffee in Split, before the palace fills.

linger:The Riva.name: The Riva
linger:The Riva.teaser: Split's waterfront living room: white paving, palms, and the palace's south wall at your back
linger:The Riva.story: The Riva runs along the south face of the palace, the wall where Diocletian's rooms once looked straight onto the water. Its present form is the Zagreb studio 3LHD's: a competition won in 2005, opened on 7 May 2007, Sudamja day, with pale concrete slabs, low green islands of Mediterranean planting and white awnings over the café tables. Sit with a coffee or a glass of Pošip and the whole port moves past: ferries for Brač and Hvar, island catamarans, fishermen heading for Matejuška. Step through to the Prokurative behind, the long arcaded square begun in 1859 to Vicko Andrić's design.
linger:The Riva.why: An hour at a Riva table is how Split watches itself; go before the works start.
facts: The waterfront below the palace's south wall, from the Prokurative (Trg Republike) east to the ferry port

linger:Matejuška with a bottle.name: Matejuška with a bottle
linger:Matejuška with a bottle.teaser: No bar, no waiter: the fishermen's harbour at dusk, a bottle, and half of Split on the quay
linger:Matejuška with a bottle.story: At the western end of the Riva the paving gives way to the small fishermen's harbour of Matejuška, where wooden gajete and pasaras lie nose to the quay and nets dry on the stone. Toward evening people drift down with a bottle from a shop, some pršut in paper and a few tomatoes, and sit on the blocks with their legs over the water while the light goes behind Marjan. Nobody serves you and nobody moves you on. Out of season it is a neighbourhood thing; in summer the crowd is younger and thicker. Fife, across the road, is the place if you want a plate.
linger:Matejuška with a bottle.why: The one stretch of Split waterfront where you sit with locals, not with a menu.
facts: Matejuška, the fishermen's harbour at the west end of the Riva, below Veli Varoš

drink:Plavac Mali.name: Plavac Mali
drink:Plavac Mali.teaser: Little blue: the dark, warm red of every Dalmatian table, grown on slopes that face the sea
drink:Plavac Mali.story: Plavac Mali means little blue, for the small dark berries. It is the red you will be poured from Split to the islands, and at its best it comes from the south face of the Pelješac peninsula, where Dingač and Postup drop steeply toward the water. DNA work showed it to be the child of Tribidrag, the grape the world knows as Zinfandel, and Dobričić from the island of Šolta, a few miles off Split. Its story is told in the history fold. In the glass it is ripe, dried-cherry fruit, grippy tannin and alcohol that often passes 14%.
drink:Plavac Mali.why: Drink it with peka lamb or brodet, when its weight and tannin have something to hold on to.
facts: Deep ruby, dried cherry and fig, firm tannin, 14% and up

drink:Pošip.name: Pošip
drink:Pošip.teaser: Korčula's white, protected in 1967 before any other Croatian white wine
drink:Pošip.story: Pošip grows almost only on Korčula, in the linked fields of Čara and Smokvica at the island's centre. Island tradition says Marin Tomašić of Smokvica found the vine in the nineteenth century; the sources disagree on the year. In 1967 it became the first Croatian white wine given legal protection of origin. DNA shows it to be a cross of two other Korčula grapes, Bratkovina and Zlatarica blatska. It makes a broad white with soft acidity, citrus peel, apricot, almond and a salty last note, fresh from steel or rounder from the barrel.
drink:Pošip.why: The white with weight enough for grilled fish, crni rižot or a plate of Pag cheese.
facts: Straw gold, citrus peel, apricot, almond, a saline finish; soft acidity

drink:Tribidrag.name: Tribidrag
drink:Tribidrag.teaser: The grape California calls Zinfandel, made again by a dozen families in Kaštela, just west of Split
drink:Tribidrag.story: The grape that became Zinfandel in California and Primitivo in Puglia is back in bottle where it was found, in the Kaštela villages strung along the bay between Split and Trogir. Twelve local growers now carry the Kaštelanski crljenak origin label, among them Anton Kovač of Putalj, whose vines climb the slopes of Kozjak above Kaštel Sućurac and who shows visitors the barrel room, the Matela family next door, and Kaštel Sikuli in Kaštel Novi. Expect a lighter, juicier red than a California Zin: red cherry, pepper, a dry finish. The story of how it was found is told in the history fold.
drink:Tribidrag.why: Drink Zinfandel's ancestor fifteen minutes from where it was found, poured by the people who replanted it.
facts: Mid-ruby, red cherry and plum, pepper, fresher and less jammy than a California Zinfandel

drink:Vugava.name: Vugava
drink:Vugava.teaser: Vis's own white, called Bugava on the island, poured in a cellar cut into an old army tunnel
drink:Vugava.story: Vugava is a white grape almost nobody grows outside Vis, the farthest of the inhabited islands off Split, where they call it Bugava. It makes a full, golden, softly aromatic white, apricot and honey with a line of salt, that can take a few years in bottle. Antonio Lipanović is the name you will find most easily: the largest grower, he ages his wine in a tunnel the Yugoslav army cut into the island, and pours Vugava, Plavac Mali and Prošek there. On Vis, Roki's, Senjanović and Ivčević also make it; on Brač, Stina is the rare exception.
drink:Vugava.why: Bring a bottle home: outside Vis you will rarely see it on a list.
facts: Golden, apricot, honey, Mediterranean herbs, saline; full and soft

drink:Prošek.name: Prošek
drink:Prošek.teaser: A sweet wine of sun-dried grapes, not a sparkling, whatever the name sounds like
drink:Prošek.story: Prošek is made by laying grapes out on racks until they shrivel, then pressing the concentrated juice into a sweet, amber or garnet wine of around 14%: Plavac Mali for the red, Maraština or Bogdanuša for the white. Dalmatian cooks pour it into the pašticada pot, and families open it for guests with dry figs or almonds. It has nothing to do with Prosecco, the Italian sparkling wine, but the names collide. The EU refused to protect Prošek in 2013; in 2021 the Commission took Croatia's new application as admissible and published it, and Italy objected. We found no final ruling.
drink:Prošek.why: A small glass at the end of dinner, with rožata or a few dried figs.
facts: Amber or garnet, raisin, dried fig, honey; sweet, around 14%

drink:Rakija.name: Rakija
drink:Rakija.teaser: Plum, pear, walnut or a fistful of island herbs, at 40% and at any hour
drink:Rakija.story: Rakija is the clear fruit spirit of the whole region, and every house seems to have a bottle. Šljivovica is plum; kruškovac pear; orahovac is dark and bitter-sweet from green walnuts; medica is softened with honey. The Dalmatian one is travarica: grape spirit steeped with sage, rosemary, fennel and whatever grows on the hill, sometimes with the sprigs left in the bottle. A farmer's bottle from the market often beats the supermarket one. Zadar's Maraska, a postwar company heir to the city's old maraschino trade, is the familiar industrial label.
drink:Rakija.why: Accept the glass when it is offered; it is how a Dalmatian host says welcome.
facts: Clear or golden, around 40%; travarica smells of sage and rosemary

bars:Paradox.name: Paradox
bars:Paradox.teaser: Taste Dalmatia against the continent: Dingač beside a Plešivica sparkler, cheese on the board
bars:Paradox.story: Use Paradox to taste across the map in one sitting: a Dingač or Postup from Pelješac, a Pošip from Korčula, then something from the cool north, a Plešivica sparkling wine or a continental white, with Pag cheese between glasses. Ask the person pouring to line up three Plavac Mali from different slopes and the difference in sun shows at once. It is the after-dinner stop more than the aperitif.
bars:Paradox.why: The one place to compare Croatia's coast and continent glass by glass.
facts: A Plavac Mali from Dingač, a Korčula Pošip and a Pag cheese board

bars:Zinfandel.teaser: Where to taste Kaštela's Tribidrag in the old town, next to a Babić from the north
bars:Zinfandel.story: The bar is named after the grape, so start there: a glass of Tribidrag from Kaštela, then a Plavac Mali to taste the child against its parent.
